questions.a: Because in Playwright “visible” means the element has a box and isn’t hidden by its own CSS. A button under a modal passes that. What catches it is a real click, which checks the element is the one that would receive the event, or elementFromPoint at its centre. Assert the action, not the state.

questions.q: “The agent writes the test and the fix. Can’t it just write a test that passes?”
questions.a: That’s why red comes first and the failure has to match the report: a test that passes on broken code is rejected before any edit. The revert run catches a test that passes regardless of the fix. For high-stakes changes, a hidden acceptance test written by someone else is the final word.

questions.q: “Screenshot tests are flaky. Why would I trust them?”
questions.a: They’re flaky when the environment moves: fonts, anti-aliasing, animations, live data, a different OS. Run them in a pinned container, turn off animations, mask dates and avatars, and set a small pixel threshold. Then prove it: the same page twice must diff to zero. And use them for regressions against a known-good image, not for judging a brand-new screen.

teach.title: When the checker looks at pixels

questions.q: “How does a text-only model ‘see’ a page?”
questions.a: Through what the browser reports as text: the accessibility tree (roles, names, states), console errors, failed network requests, the DOM, and numbers from layout (boxes, computed styles, what elementFromPoint returns). That covers behaviour, interaction and geometry, which is most front-end bugs.

teach.title: The ladder: the cheapest check that can see the bug

questions.q: “When does the coding model itself need vision?”
questions.a: When the input is an image: the bug report is a screenshot, the task is “build this mock”, or the interface is a canvas. Then the model that understands the task has to read pixels. When the task is in words and only the check is visual, a vision model can sit at the end as the checker instead.

questions.q: “How would you know whether the vision checker is any good?”
questions.a: Build a small set of screens with defects you planted on purpose, plus clean ones. Measure misses (said fine, wasn’t) and false alarms separately, and run each screen a few times to see whether the verdict changes. The miss rate decides whether it can block a merge or only add a comment. Guide 0019 covers why one overall agreement number hides exactly this.

questions.q: “Isn’t this too slow for an agent loop?”
questions.a: Run only the reproduction during the loop: one test, one browser, a few seconds. Run the rest at the end: other sizes, other engines, the existing suite, any screenshot or vision checks. Unit tests stay in the loop too, for logic, because they are fast and they still catch what they can see.

teach.title: The fundamentals, in plain words first

questions.q: “The bug only happens sometimes. Now what?”
questions.a: Make the timing part of the test: slow the network, throttle the CPU, wait on the condition rather than a fixed delay, and repeat the run until it reproduces. Record a trace (Playwright’s trace viewer stores each step’s DOM and a screenshot) so the agent can read what was on screen at the moment it failed.

questions.q: “Should the agent read screenshots while it debugs, even for behaviour bugs?”
questions.a: It can help a model that is good at it, but it isn’t free. Images cost many more tokens than an accessibility snapshot, and a long run full of screenshots fills the context with near-duplicates, the problem guide 0016 is about. Default to text, and take a screenshot when the next decision depends on how the page looks.

teach.title: So, do you need a multimodal model?

questions.a: It comes free with doing this well. Finding elements by role and name means the test fails if a screen reader couldn’t find them either. Add an automated scan for rule violations, and know its limit: it finds missing labels and low contrast, not whether the flow is usable without a mouse.

questions.q: “What does the agent hand the reviewer?”
questions.a: The diff, the reproduction test, its red and green runs with the failure message, the revert result, the browsers and sizes covered, and a before-and-after screenshot pair for a person to glance at. The screenshot is for the human. The verdict comes from the test.

teach.title: Five checks, and one is the gate

questions.q: “How do you know this is working across hundreds of fixes?”
questions.a: Track the share of UI fixes that came with a fail-to-pass reproduction, the share whose failure matched the report, the vision checker’s miss rate on planted defects, and the escape rate: UI bugs reopened after the agent marked them verified. Escapes, read by hand, show which rung was missing.
